title: Usability Testing
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Usability Testing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Usability testing is an evaluative method in which representative participants attempt realistic activities with a product or prototype while researchers observe what happens. It reveals how the interface, content, system behaviour, and context support or obstruct action.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at what usability testing reveals?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The unit of analysis is not whether a person “likes the design.” It is the encounter between a person, a goal, and a designed system. Evidence includes where participants begin, what they expect, which information they use, hesitations, wrong turns, recovery, completion, time where meaningful, assistance needed, confidence, and interpretation after the task.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Testing can expose defects in comprehension, navigation, feedback, control mapping, workflow, content, and recovery. It cannot by itself establish market demand, long-term retention, the prevalence of a problem in the whole population, clinical effectiveness, or why non-users never arrived.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A small qualitative study is particularly good at discovering and diagnosing breakdowns; it is generally poor at estimating how common each breakdown is.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Do not call it “testing users.” The participant is not being graded. The design and its assumptions are under examination.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Design the study around decisions and tasks
turns.text: What changes when we look at design the study around decisions and tasks?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A useful test begins before recruitment.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: 1. State the decision and research questions. Separate broad questions from observable behaviours. “Is it intuitive?” is vague. “Can participants explain why this specialist was recommended and identify the unknown cost before committing?” is testable. 2. Define relevant participants.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Recruit for behaviours, knowledge, access needs, and circumstances that affect the task—not convenient demographics alone. Include people commonly excluded by the service. 3. Choose the test object. Existing product, competitor, paper flow, clickable prototype, coded slice, or whole service. Document its limitations. 4. Write scenarios, not instructions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Give a believable motivation without naming controls or revealing the route. “Your GP has referred you and you need an appointment compatible with work and step-free access” is better than “open Filters and select Accessibility.” 5. Select tasks and order. Prioritise consequential, uncertain tasks. Avoid making an earlier task teach the answer to a later one.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Include a boundary or recovery path. 6. Define evidence in advance. Note what counts as success, partial success, failure, assistance, critical misunderstanding, and abandonment. Decide which measures are useful without pretending they are more precise than the study allows. 7. Pilot.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A pilot catches broken links, leading wording, unrealistic data, timing problems, and prototype gaps before participant time is wasted.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at moderate without teaching the interface?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Begin with consent, recording choices, confidentiality, the participant’s right to stop, and reassurance that the product—not the person—is being tested. Establish context before the tasks. During the session, invite participants to think aloud when that will help, but recognise that verbalising can change pace and attention.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use neutral prompts: “What are you thinking?” “What did you expect?” “What does that mean to you?” Avoid praise that signals a correct answer, questions that contain the desired interpretation, and rapid rescue.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: When a participant becomes stuck, observe long enough to understand the breakdown, then use a pre-planned assistance ladder: repeat the scenario, ask what they would do outside the study, offer a small neutral prompt, and only then move them forward. Record the level of help.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Moderation is not passive silence. In sensitive settings it includes care. Stop or redirect if the scenario causes distress, avoid collecting unnecessary health information, and debrief simulated consequences clearly.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at analyse behaviour without flattening it?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Debrief after each session while context is fresh. Separate observation (“participant opened clinic details after choosing”) from interpretation (“important access information may arrive too late”) and recommendation (“surface step-free status in the option”). Triangulate recordings, notes, interaction data, and participants’ explanations.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Look for patterns, but do not use frequency alone. One rare failure can be critical if it risks missed care, money, privacy, or exclusion. Conversely, repeated hesitation may be low consequence. Judge findings through consequence, reach, recoverability, confidence, and strategic relevance.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Include successful strategies too; they reveal what should not be damaged during iteration.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: changing a flight?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A participant successfully selects a new flight but does not realise the change is unconfirmed until payment. Task completion alone would mark success; the mental model reveals risk. A good protocol observes whether the traveller understands fare difference, connection impact, and finality, and includes recovery when a seat disappears.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The important outcome is not clicks completed but a correct, confident, recoverable change.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at failure modes and limits?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Scripted tasks: wording tells participants where to click and masks findability problems. Convenience recruiting: colleagues or confident digital users stand in for affected people. Moderator rescue: help arrives before the breakdown becomes visible. Opinion collection: discussion replaces attempted behaviour.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Prototype blindness: missing data or interactions alter behaviour but are ignored in analysis. Count as prevalence: five sessions are used to make population estimates. Happy-path testing: recovery, accessibility, delay, and consequential edge states disappear. Finding inflation: every hesitation becomes a defect without considering consequence.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior practice connects test scope to decision risk. Use formative studies early to improve a concept; use summative or benchmark studies only when the design, measures, sample, and conditions support comparison. Combine usability evidence with analytics, accessibility evaluation, operational data, field research, and outcome measures when the decision requires them.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Make observation a team capability, but protect participant dignity. Stakeholders should receive behaviour-focused note templates and ground rules, not a spectacle. Track which populations and contexts have not been represented.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: For healthcare, finance, government, and other consequential services, define escalation routes for safety or safeguarding concerns before sessions begin.

turns.speaker: guide

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: an account-recovery flow. Give participants a realistic reason to regain access, not an instruction to click “Forgot password.” Watch where they hesitate, what they believe has happened after requesting a link, and whether they can recover from an expired one.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A completed task matters, but so do confidence, wrong turns, and the moderator's influence on behaviour.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Watch someone use a familiar product without coaching them. Record the first moment their expectation and the system response diverge. What did they expect, what evidence did the interface provide, how did they recover, and what would you need to learn before recommending a change?
